en: The Great Commentary on the Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sutra: Maxims, Volume One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Baiting Shanyue of Siming. ○ The First Fascicle of the Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sutra Commentary.

(Section One: The Primordial) Our Buddha expounded the Great Canon of Teachings, which was upheld by Ānanda; the Wise One (Zhiyi) composed the heroic texts of the Three Sections, which would not have been compiled were it not for Zhizhe (Zhanran).
Had these words not been compiled, they surely would not have reached the present day.
Were it not for this transmission and preservation, how could our Buddha’s teachings be shown to future generations? How profound indeed is the Way of our Buddhas and Patriarchs!
Where there are such sages and worthies, there must necessarily be such compositions;

it is just as the Master [Confucius] taught his disciples, who recorded his virtuous words to be handed down to future generations. Thus we know that the sages of the past and the worthies of the present mutually effect transformation through a single principle.
This is the reason for recording this private account, and its general outline is twofold: first, praising the Master.

The Virtuous Master has clarified these matters through ten general points; if one examines the latter five, they appear somewhat redundant and are not essential, so it suffices merely to accept or reject them according to one's own virtue.
Second, regarding the formal exposition of the causal origin (*nidāna*), the sequence of listening follows next;
as for the arrangement of the remaining sections, students should understand this for themselves without waiting for a detailed discussion.
(515) How great are these words! Their purport is such that they will surely demonstrate [the ultimate], taking the rational nature (*dharmatā*) as their fundamental basis.

To speak of the realization of the ultimate is precisely the primary beginning of this sutra; thus, the Profound Preface states: "The 'Original Ground' (*mūlabhūmi*) refers to the ground of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Even the 'beginning of the beginningless' is insufficient to describe its limit; it is as if viewing a point of dust before kalpas as numerous as motes of dust."

Regarding what has been discussed over these two nights—that whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and characteristics of reality are eternally thus—the profound treasury likewise praises the subtlety of this Dharma.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The treasury of the *Dharmaparyāya* is deep, firm, remote, and far-reaching; no one can reach it.

Yet, it is also not something that can be approached from afar or near, nor is it easy or difficult to recognize its ultimate point. Therefore, it is said: "This Dharma cannot be shown; its verbal expressions are quiescent."
If one knows that the phenomena of the world are not permanent, then [the truth] will be fully manifested right where one stands;

how could it be far away? Thus, who is it that realizes this principle? Therefore, it is said: "That which all Buddhas of the three periods have realized," and again, "This is the foremost quiescence, known at the site of enlightenment. Now, as for this "knowing," it is the ultimate realization.

This is what is meant. Because of realization, one is able to have discourse; this is why the Buddha, according to the times, establishes his transformation (teaching), so that all living beings may likewise attain this realization, and only then does he cease.
Therefore it is said: "The great causal condition," and so forth. Thus, sentient beings use this cause to evoke the Buddha, and the Buddha uses this condition to arise in response;
this is precisely the meaning of "causal conditions" as they apply here. When [beings] first see my body, they enter...

The Buddha’s wisdom consists of those with superior faculties and sharp intelligence who enter the Sudden Teaching first; as for those of inferior capacity, they cannot avoid being guided by other teachings through gradual adaptation.

Thus, there is the teaching of expedient means and provisional inclusion. When the time comes at Vulture Peak to reveal and manifest the ultimate truth, one abandons the previous expedients and speaks only of the One Vehicle to express this principle to its fullest extent; yet fundamentally, there is no dharma to be abandoned.

Furthermore, this term "Cloud" is spoken in contrast to the provisional teachings of the past; in reality, the present sutra reveals the ultimate truth beyond all relativity, wherein there is no distinction whatsoever.

Therefore, it is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Now, as for "wondrous Dharma" (*miao fa*): "wondrous" means that there is no other wondrousness apart from this, which is what makes it a "Dharma.
"Dharma" means that there is no other Dharma apart from this, which is what makes it "wondrous. It is for this reason that—

When a single wondrous character (*myōji*) penetrates them all, then the purport of this title, the text of this treatise, and the Dharma of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses are none other than wondrous;
for each and every phenomenon, in its very essence, is the perfect fusion of the three truths.

Therefore it is said that "wondrous" refers to the wondrous nature of the provisional and real teachings of one's own practice (*jigyō*). Since every single phenomenon is thus wondrous, the Lotus Flower is cited [as the symbol].

Furthermore, the reason the lotus flower is used as a metaphor for the provisional and the real teachings involves three meanings—originality and trace, manifestation and opening, and abolition—and the three pairs of provisional and real, such as self and other.
When it specifically speaks of "one's own practice," it means that because [the truth] is revealed and made manifest, all that pertains to transforming others is none other than one's own practice;
how then could a distinction between self and other remain? This is just like the case of the original and the trace.
Whether in terms of provisional or ultimate truth, whether in title or text, all converge upon this single word "wondrous" (miao).
This most excellent *sūtra* further clarifies the intent of manifesting the wondrous through excellence—the meaning of the ultimate manifestation of the wondrous.
It is therefore termed the "Gate of Ambrosia," which is precisely the gate entered by this present sutra.

(Xuan Yi 17) The original arrangement of these chapters was intended to arouse the mind so as to reach the gates and establish their names; thus, by opening up the profound and advancing from the beginning, one comes to know that the Patriarch’s intent was deeply penetrating.
Even a single word or a single meaning, down to the minutiae of a single topical section, is not in vain.
As now, at the head of this chapter, seven sections are listed: they give rise to the five minds, accomplish the five faculties, and eliminate the five obstacles. Thus it begins.

Furthermore, it is said that the entry into the three gates of liberation is the path, and the establishment of the sages is the source; this is intended to open up the profound and advance the beginner.
It is held that the profound principle does not begin without names, and initial practice does not progress without words.

From the beginning to the end, everything is attained from this—how could this be a small matter? Sight and hearing rely upon sound and form; thus, the two teachings cause one to follow their respective paths.

Is it not essential that one traces the manifestations to reach the ultimate principle? Thus we know that every single dharma and meaning is established for the sake of the student’s entry into the Way;

how could they compare to the defects of later generations’ rigid categorization—dividing this as "A" and that as "B," causing hundreds or thousands of people to be needlessly disturbed? This is something that must be understood at the very beginning of entering the text.
(Section 17 of Xuanyi) The three truths are but one. If even "one" does not exist, how much less can one speak of difference? How could there be any distinction between the coarse and the subtle?

It is solely because the teachings differ in being partial or complete, and the times differ in being ancient or modern—due to these differences in whether [the truth] is revealed or unrevealed—that the coarse and the subtle are distinguished.
Regarding the present text, it is said that the sequential three truths are the coarse dharma, while the perfectly integrated three truths are the subtle.
It is the wondrous Dharma; it is also called this wondrous truth, which fundamentally possesses what is known as the innate nature and virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

Yet, when spoken of in terms of its fundamental existence, it has never undergone increase or decrease. Because each dharma abides in its own dharma-position, the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
However, if one uses this principle of eternal abiding to clarify the worldly phenomena, it is easy; whereas if one uses worldly phenomena to clarify this principle, it is difficult.
To claim that characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are eternally abiding is difficult to establish, for characteristics are things with which human sentiment is habitually familiar;
thus, to clarify their underlying principle is not it difficult? One must realize that each phenomenon (*dharma*) abides in its own dharma-position (*dharmasthiti*);

in this way, characteristics are eternally abiding, making the principle somewhat easier to understand. This is as clear as the analogy of the wondrous joy of waves and water. Indeed, this is the intended meaning of the revelation.

One should fundamentally regulate the emotions through principle rather than allow the emotions to obscure the principle; students ought to forget their emotions and investigate deeply so as to attain realization within themselves.
(Xuan Yi 18) Since the teachings of the Tathāgata’s five periods throughout his lifetime first appear here, the *Xuanyi* states: "The establishment of the initial teaching."
Integration and non-integration do not exceed the two paths of integration and distinction; therefore, they are discussed in contrast to one another.
However, since capacities may be small or great and teachings may be inclusive or exclusive, it is not necessary for them to be directed solely in one way.

Because a single direction would be insufficient to lead those of small capacity into the Great Vehicle, there are instances where both are mentioned, instances where only one is mentioned, and instances where integration is used to critique non-integration.

Regarding those who have "reliance," as opposed to those who lack it, there is further a distinction between "perfect fusion" (*yuánróng*) and "penetrating fusion" (*róngtōng*) within the two flavors.
Upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, all things are fused; the revelation of the three truths is none other than the One Vehicle.

However, when "perfect fusion" is contrasted with "non-fusion," it refers to the distinction between the partial and the perfect; when "penetrating fusion" is contrasted with "non-fusion," it refers to the distinction between the Small and the Great Vehicles.
The meaning cannot be discussed in general terms; the rest is as explained in the *Zhan* (commentary), etc. (Xuan 18).

Regarding the One Vehicle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-sheng*): when one is not yet capable of hearing [the teaching] that it is "solely one," why is it that hearing [it as] "only one" constitutes slander, whereas hearing [it as] "also three" does not?

This is also not easy to understand. Now, I say that "also three" necessarily implies the simultaneous presentation of the partial and the perfect; although for that person, [the teaching of] the perfect is not...
It is appropriate that there are still partial aspects through which one may enter; therefore, one discards what is inappropriate and follows what is appropriate.
If, however, one hears only a single [extreme] view, it will forever conflict with their aspirations, and thus they slander it. It is like serving food and presenting two flavors:
if someone dislikes what is delicious but, conversely, craves what is unpalatable, their preferences for acceptance and rejection will differ. This is the case if only one flavor is presented.
If it is of a single flavor yet not what one desires, and one does not even eat it, how could one avoid slandering it? Such is the principle;
however, if explained according to the secret and hidden [teachings], then it does not fall within the category of those who hear.

(Stele Text 30) Now, in explaining the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one must necessarily distinguish between the "coarse" and the "subtle," with differing interpretations based on either the classification of the sūtras (*bù*) or the classification of the teachings (*jiào*), as is clearly explained in the usual commentaries (etc.).
If we rely on the current sūtra, there is no other teaching [superior to it], so while the two-fold distinction might not be necessary;

nevertheless, because it is contrasted with the past [teachings] which possess both the partial (*piān*) and the complete (*yuán*), the classification by teaching (*jiào*) serves only to select the partial, whereas the classification by sūtra (*bù*)—encompassing both the partial and the complete—is divided into these two distinct categories. Thus, the "complete" of the past...
Because it involves a combination of *nikāyas*, it is not "wondrous"; because the teaching has no distinction between "this" and "that," it is wondrous. To illustrate this by analogy:
the "coarse person" is like the partial [teaching] and the "subtle person" is like the perfect [teaching]. Yet both possess faults:

the perfect [teaching] has the fault of concealing the provisional, while the partial [teaching] has the fault of hiding the real. Therefore, both are not [ultimately true]; thus, the meaning of the "perfect" from the past has something to be compared with.
To "take away" (duo) is still a minor matter and does not mean something coarse; it refers to having faults that prevent one from being established with a sublime name.

This is just like the distinction between a gentleman and a petty person, which is naturally fixed: because a gentleman competes with a petty person, he cannot be without fault—this can be understood by analogy.
(Section 19 of Xuan) The Dharma has coarse and subtle aspects, and the analogy is likewise; this is why these flowers are used as examples for the coarse and subtle.
Coarse flowers refer to the "wild flowers. Generally, six types of flowers are listed to illustrate six kinds of people.

However, if one speaks of people by way of the Dharma in a comprehensive sense, then the four periods and three teachings prior [to the Lotus Sutra] are all included. Because the provisional and real Dharmas differ, they are thus illustrated.
How could coarse flowers compare to the lotus, which possesses both marvelous blossoms and fruit, and carries the meaning that even as the lotus forms, it also falls?
This is used as an analogy for the present sutra’s principle that the provisional and the real are mutually identical, as well as its state of being neither provisional nor real.

Speaking from this perspective, the so-called "three analogies of the lotus" from antiquity—which all illustrate the wondrous Dharma of the present sutra as belonging to the same essence—are fundamentally based upon this very point.
This is because these phrases are stated in accordance with the specific intent of the present Sautrāntika school.

Otherwise, since the "coarse flower" was already used as a metaphor for the dharmas of people in the past, how could the "lotus flower" be applied as a metaphor for the bestowal of expedient means (*upāya*)? It would be improper to employ two metaphors for the same four seasons; therefore, this point must be clarified.
(Section 19 of Xuán) The analogy that "the flower exists for the sake of the lotus" clarifies the meaning of the identity of essence (*tongti*) through the equality of the real and the provisional.

Furthermore, it is said that "opening that which covers" is explained in terms of the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings (*jīqíng*). Former scholars maintained that the three analogies belong to the identity of essence while the capacities and inclinations belong to the diversity of essence;
they thus considered identity and diversity to be contradictory. They failed to realize that since both [concepts] arise from the present text, why should one specifically be treated as distinct?
Regarding the interpretation of the meaning, speaking from the present perspective, there is no great difference; compared to the Chinese version, there is nothing particularly extraordinary.

One may call it "identical" based on the fact that the *Lotus Sūtra* (Lianhua) clarifies this through its own opening and closing structures. However, speaking from the perspective of what is perceived, one may call it "different," for what is perceived is precisely the functioning of the mind and its dispositions (*jìqíng*).
Thus, we know that the textual intent must be rooted in the fundamental source and the general principle. If the similarities and differences are clearly understood, [the truth] will be attained.

The inscription states: "The teachings for humans and the principles of reality share the same principle; therefore, they are equally merged within the three virtues. It is not that provisional and ultimate truths are unequal;
rather, all are so because this is the natural state of the supreme limit. Until one accords with this ultimate principle, it will remain difficult to speak of their convergence."
(19) The *Shū* uses the "substance" (*tai*) to explain the "ritual" (*rei*); here, we borrow this to explain the "substance.

Using the "substance" to explain the "ritual" correctly takes up the principle that the relationships of ruler and subject, father and son, possess a hierarchy of honor and lowliness, yet all equally abide by the laws of ritual. Using the "ritual" to explain the "substance" correctly speaks of good and evil;
although there are differences between delusion and awakening, nothing whatsoever transcends the *dharmatā*. Therefore it is said, etc. Some older [commentaries] take the following text...
Regarding the differing views on whether [the teachings] are opened or discarded—such as those who say that the Buddha’s vision and other such doubts are now resolved—it is said that this is not so.

One must understand that whenever the term "essence" (*tǐ*) is used, regardless of whether it concerns the present or the past, or whether the teaching is opened or discarded, one must always explain it in this way. As Siming said:
"Although the essence of *dharmatā* pervades all things, its meaning is restricted to the realization of the fruit; is this not precisely [the point]?"
This is identical to the present text; however, since that [earlier] teaching still applies to the present, it establishes the principle of "opening" and "abandoning.

Thus, without relying on the opening of provisional means (*upāya*), one cannot manifest that the essence of this sutra pervades all things; and without clarifying the abandoning of provisional means, one cannot see that this essence is wondrously ultimate within all phenomena.
Therefore, we know that these two meanings are in fact consistent with one another in principle. How can one arbitrarily create distinctions between them to accept or reject?

Regarding this, if one were to say that this passage does not discuss the opening and setting aside [of provisional teachings], then even if it were not the primary text, how could it fail to encompass the essential?

One must know that this passage precisely reveals the subtlety of the opening and manifestation of the present sutra; why would it be otherwise? This is explained in detail in the *Lèilùn* (Treatise on Classification), and so forth.

(Section 10: Profundity and Unity) Regarding the realization that the span of life is neither identical to nor different [from its essence], this is now the testimony to the substance of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Commentators call this "citing the same" (*yitong*). That which is neither identical to nor different is precisely the Middle Way as the essence;

therefore, when expressed in terms of negation and illumination, it is appropriate to call it the fundamental realization upon which the distant lifespan depends, and thus fitting for it to be the true reality. Nevertheless, the essence of the three realms is one. And yet—
What each person perceives differs; when comparing their words regarding the true essence (*dharmatā*), which one accords with reality? This, too, cannot yet be definitively settled.
From the perspective of what each perceives—such as difference and so forth—each claims to accord with reality, and thus it may be said that they are "accordant.
However, from the perspective of the three realms as perceived by each, there has never been a fixed certainty; it is simply the inconceivable and wondrous essence.

Thus, it is said that there is nothing that is "appropriate" (*dangke*). However, since what is seen by the nine realms is delusion and what is seen by the Buddha is reality, the Buddha’s vision of the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—which accords with the fundamental nature and is the ultimate realization—may also be called appropriate.
Nevertheless, even when one calls something appropriate, it has never actually been appropriate; and even when one calls something inappropriate, it has never actually been inappropriate.
One should simply say that there is neither "appropriate" nor "inappropriate," for how could I possibly know it? This is precisely why it constitutes the correct essence of the present scripture.
(Xuan Yi 10) The commentary states:
Since both wisdom and its object are called the "true mark" (*dharmatā*), one attains the text in order to observe wisdom and realize the essence.
As previously cited, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, as well as his ability to perceive the characteristics of the triple world, are all based on this principle.

Because this principle is not easily clarified, it is manifested by means of its functional capacity (*neng*). If one were to discuss this essence (*ti*) alone, it would manifest the inherent virtue of the nature;
thus, one must take the single nature as the essence in order to speak of the "essence of the nature. If, however, one takes what is manifested as the functional capacity, then...
Although Chengzong’s conception of the essence of the family is not the primary intent here, it nevertheless cannot be dismissed;
while the explanation according to the *Xiuzhen men* is intended primarily for later generations to cultivate this essence, there is no contradiction in it also encompassing this meaning.

(Section 10: Profound Unity) Now, taking the three truths in their perfect fusion as the true essence of the *dharmakāya*, [the author] cites the teaching of Vajragarbha on "extremely subtle wisdom" as proof.
Although the phrasing differs, the intent is the same; however, since the first two phrases merely concern emptiness and existence, how could they jointly serve as proof for the essence of the sutra?
Therefore, the *Shiki* (Commentary) states that one should interpret the meaning of these two phrases such that the speaker, regarding the preceding two phrases, [proceeds as follows...]
When the wondrous emptiness and the wondrous provisional are demonstrated, the principle of the three truths in their perfect fusion is established.

Although it is said that they are "equal," the words differ while the meaning remains the same; thus, the significance lies in their sharing a single substance. Yet, regarding the two phrases of emptiness and the provisional, what is their substance and meaning?

This is because it is difficult to separate them from their union; therefore, in the response, the union is explained by means of separation, stating: "As for 'inconceivable'... and so forth. Since it is already called "inconceivable," [it cannot be grasped by conceptual thought].
When one deliberates upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*), these constitute the perfect fusion of the three truths (*triratna-satyam*).

Because raising one immediately encompasses the three, the provisional and emptiness possess the meaning of being identical with the Middle (*madhyama*), and the Middle possesses the meaning of containing both emptiness and the provisional. Although these aspects involve both inclusion and exclusion, they all take the Middle as their essence, for one must necessarily reject cultivation (*bhāvanā*) to realize the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).

For those who wish to know this in detail, they should consult Zhiyi’s *Guangming jing wenju ji* (Notes on the Meaning of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*) and the *Lunlei* (Categorization of Doctrines). You should look into these yourself.
It is known that one need not trouble oneself with further elaboration.

(Xuan Yi 10) Previously, it was stated that refusing to accept [the teaching] constitutes slander; here, it is stated that failing to understand it constitutes slander. Although there is a difference between the internal and external, or the shallow and the deep, as far as the Dharma itself is concerned, they are one and the same.
Nevertheless, there is no lack of distinction regarding what is granted or withheld. The current text does not state that there are four types; rather, it refers to "denying" and "non-existence."

This is because they give rise to attachments toward the Dharma and engage in arbitrary conceptualizations that result in error; though they have received the internal teachings, their views become those of outsiders—what are called "non-Buddhists who study the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, they deviate from the true nature of reality (dharmatā) and give rise to demonic views, asserting that everything other than the true nature of reality is the work of Māra.
If they persist in these attachments without relinquishing them, how could they avoid falling into slander?

It is indeed a tragedy that the Dharma has fallen into such a state; yet it may also be said that those who do not accept it simply lack faith, and it is not necessarily the case that they hold onto their views to form slander.
As for those who currently slander [the Dharma], although its basis is the internal teaching (Buddhism), their transgressions are far greater than others.

(Section 11: Xuanyi) Generally speaking, what I term "private" [explanations] necessarily assist in elucidating the original text; even when not assisting in its explicit manifestation, they must nonetheless accord with the intent of the text.

To call this "private" is to mean that these are not separate, independent treatises. Furthermore, is it not the case that there is a profound significance in specifically adding these private explanations hereafter?
It is because the preceding section clarified the avoidance of slander as a means to distinguish the incorrect, yet it did not explicitly discuss the nature of that slander.
Who is it that can break [these views], and by what means? It is said that they are broken crosswise through the four attachments of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth.
Thus one knows that those previously referred to as "deniers" are precisely these ordinary beings and the followers of the Three Vehicles whom we now refute.

As for the refuter, it is simply the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Therefore, it is said that the principle of emptiness and existence is precisely the refutation of these proofs and so forth; moreover, if one were to simplify this:
If it were not subsumed, the Dharma would have no place of return and people would treat it as discarded refuse; what, then, does this present sutra reveal? Therefore it is said:

"Since it does not accord with the true essence, under which dharma is it categorized? Thus, the previous attachments to mere emptiness and so forth are themselves subsumed within the three pairs of provisional and real;
in principle, there is nothing that is not a skillful means within the essence. This is precisely what the present sutra reveals, and for this reason, there is further [discussion].
Regarding the term "substance" (*ti*), the purport of the subsequent section is that one should know the text contains both inclusion and simplification, as well as refutation and reconciliation;

thus, there are many ways it assists in the exegesis. Let the reader examine this carefully. Xuánzàng says: "Substance and transformation, the provisional and the real, etc."—this is a direct demonstration of the opening of the provisional.

Zǐqiān states: "The 'substance' of 'thoroughly understanding substance' is so called because it is understood through the opening [of the provisional]. Although these words are easy to speak, the underlying principle is indeed profound.

It is difficult to clarify; one should know that fundamentally there is but a single principle. Because the teachings are established in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings (*tad-ālambana*), they are divided into three distinct forms.

Now, this sutra reveals and clarifies [the truth], pointing out that the provisional (*upāya*) is itself the real (*bhūta*). It also causes those of the perfect capacity (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) to realize it in accordance with their nature (*dharmatā*); hence it is said, "and so forth.

What is called the provisional and the real for the sake of transforming others is likewise the principle of mere emptiness (*śūnyatā-mātra*). Even from the perspective of its own specific stage, it may be termed "real. The provisional and the real for both self and others are also...

These are spoken of in contrast to the "merely" (but) and "not merely" (not-but) emptiness; thus, although there are provisional and real [teachings] for transforming others, they are all termed "provisional," and the provisional of one's own practice is likewise merely the "merely-middle" in contrast to the Perfect, which is termed "provisional. All such provisional and real [distinctions] are now opened up [to reveal their unity];
in principle, there is nothing that is not the same essence of provisional and real, perfect and subtle—the Three Truths. One should realize and embody it in this way.
This has been attained.
If one were to discuss the Buddha’s realm, it is already difficult to express; how much more so to speak of its ultimate limit?

Since it is called "ultimate," it is said that this refers merely to the provisional and the real within the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), which describes a delimited boundary. Even if the sutra says, "Only the Buddha [knows it],"...
The Buddha’s thorough investigation and revelation of the true mark of all phenomena does not go beyond the suchness of the realm;
yet one should not immediately take it as being thus revealed. Even if it were revealed in this way, students should not interpret it accordingly.
Since it is neither revealed in this manner nor to be interpreted in this way, how is it ultimately? Simply know that because it cannot be revealed or interpreted in this way, you have understood.

(Divination Stick No. 44) Generally speaking, when discussing the establishment of transformative teachings (*śāsana*), the conditions for the occasion, and the merit of attaining benefit, it is appropriate to attribute these to the Buddha.
Yet, in this and the preceding text, the merit is specifically attributed to the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. What is the principle behind this?

One might say that while this indeed rests with the Buddha—since the reason the Buddha establishes transformative teachings and the reason sentient beings gain benefit from those conditions lie solely in the Great Function (*mahā-vyāpāra*) of his single transformation—it is nevertheless [the Sūtra].
One does not consider this a personal achievement, but attributes it to the principle of the same essence (*samatā-sarīra*); for the provisional and the real are naturally so. Thus it is said:

"If they were not of the same essence, there would be no means by which to bestow, open, or set aside [the teachings]. Yet, if transformation did not transform itself, how could the Dharma even exist?
Returning once more to the underlying principle, the Sūtra states: "All classes of beings—gods, humans, and the multitudes—rely upon this power of grace. This, indeed, arises from...

This is what is meant by "principle" (*li*). Since principle is devoid of discrimination, how could it possess any power? One must surely say that human affairs are the power of man, while Heaven is the power of Heaven.
In this way, the power of the Buddha is the power of the Dharma; the power of the Dharma is the power of principle;
and the power of principle is the power of oneself. Thus, they are one and the same. How then can there be any distinction between them?
One must surely return to this [conclusion].

(Xuanzang’s *Yi Jing*, Fascicle 15, Stanza 45; Original Text, Stanza 45) Establishing the five periods as the orthodox compendium, this text describes the *Lotus Sūtra*’s exposition on faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*) while simultaneously presenting the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s doctrine of the mutual generation of the five flavors to judge the sequence and arrangement of all the scriptures; its meaning is thus clear. Furthermore...
What is the purpose of citing the *Avataṃsaka*’s "three illuminations" as proof? The *Shu-chi* (Sub-commentary) provides a detailed analysis, stating:

"In the response, first the intended meaning of each of the two passages is presented through analogy; next, the principle by which they mutually corroborate one another is clarified, stating: 'Now, in expounding the *Avataṃsaka*, etc.
This means that without the five flavors, there would be no way to develop the three and thereby complete the five. Thus it is said: 'Although their numbers are unequal,' which concludes the answer."
This is the intent of the initial question. Furthermore, it is said that by using the ox as a metaphor for the Buddha and so forth, the *Avataṃsaka* merely serves as a partial analogy.
If it were not for the "three illuminations in a single day," there would be no way to see how the five flavors all emerge from the ox;

thus, this is used as a metaphor for how all five flavors are spoken by the Buddha. Therefore, it is said that the two meanings from the two sutras are employed to mutually complete one another, thereby concluding the answer.
Next is the "Meaning" (yi), which refers to the meanings of two scriptures; there is no need to establish separate topical sections for their explanation.
(Quotation, Vol. 1, No.
47) The quotation states: "The secret [teaching] is horizontally pervasive, never failing to reach anywhere. This meaning contrasts the *Avataṃsaka* and the Deer Park [teachings] with the *Vaipulya*.

How could there possibly be a distinction between Buddhas and sentient beings, or a starting point for delusion and awakening? Why, then, do you say that all phenomena are fundamentally the Buddha-dharma?
If this were so, would not the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) also be partial? [The answer is: The principle of fundamental wondrousness is one.
It is without self-interest; precisely because it is without self-interest, it has never undergone increase or decrease—this is what is meant by "the nature and characteristics are eternally thus.
However, those who rely upon it differ in their attainment or failure. Thus, the awakened attain, while the deluded fail.
Those who attain obtain the principle of original suchness; being able to accord with this nature and realize the ultimate, this Dharma is designated as the Dharma for such persons.

Although that which is lost has never actually been lost, it is because one does not regard this person as having attained this Dharma that there is a distinction between Buddhas and [ordinary] beings.
Furthermore, it is said: "All conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are, for the Tathāgata, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This means that while the name "conventional truth" is obtained from the perspective of sentient beings, for the Buddha, there is nothing that is not the principle of the ultimate truth; fundamentally, there are no two distinct dharmas.

Therefore, we know that while the deluded are themselves deluded due to their inverted views—consequently perceiving things as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—the essence itself is not deluded and thus is nothing other than the Buddha-dharma, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, it is said: "Now, to clarify and demonstrate this, the phrase 'all dharmas' precisely indicates those very dharmas that have always existed from the beginning.
Even at the extreme limit of ordinary delusion, could there be anything that is not included among all dharmas?

The reason for the difference lies solely in whether the emotional mind (*citta*) is detached or not. Because the Buddha is detached from emotion, he perceives that all phenomena (*dharma*) are primordially devoid of characteristics;
thus, all phenomena are no longer "all phenomena. He perceives the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena as it has been revealed from the very beginning.

Therefore, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it is only when these four propositions are transcended that one may name them "all phenomena. Furthermore, the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* says: "Transcending the four..."

In the profound meaning (*xuan-yi*) of other sutras, there are only five chapters; only in this present *Xuan* (Profound Meaning) is there the distinction between the "approximate teaching" (*jiao-yue*) and the "approximate practice" (*xing-yue*), and so forth. This constitutes...

Were one to discuss them, the chapter on "Characteristics of the Teachings" (*jiàoxiàng*) would suffice to distinguish their similarities and differences—why rely on this? It is simply that other scriptures do not necessarily possess this [same structure].

Although the function preceding the essence may indeed have its factual basis, it does not necessarily possess its textual record; as for that which unites both text and fact, only this particular passage is thus.
Therefore, it is specifically employed here to clarify these two types.

The commentary on the *Śūrangama Sūtra* (the *Shiqian*) explains this briefly with two points: first, from the perspective of the Buddha’s intention; second, from the perspective of...
This knowledge of the dharma-body belongs merely to one side of self-cultivation; it is only when discussed in relation to the capacities of sentient beings that its distinct nature becomes manifest.
Therefore, the "grass hut" must be demolished; such demolition destroys the deluded attachments, not the Dharma itself.
As for that Dharma, it is of the same essence as the metaphor of the lotus flower, and is precisely what is revealed by it.

it is the Middle—why wait until one ceases to employ the mental deliberation of existence and non-existence before it is considered the Middle? Therefore, I say that this merely indicates its general direction. If...

thus, it applies equally to those of sharp and dull faculties alike. However, this [text] specifically states that it is intended solely for those of dull faculties.

(Xuan Yi 36) Now, the "First Principle" (*paramārtha*) is the ultimate discourse of the Buddha-dharma, wherein there is that which can be spoken and that which cannot be spoken.

That which can be spoken refers to the principle of the true mark (*tathatā*), which may be expressed through all phenomena by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), such as "all things are equal in reality."
Knowing that this principle has never been restricted to a single aspect, one realizes that every gate can serve as an entrance to reality. Upon entering, there is realization;
upon realizing, there is reaching the ultimate. Because the ultimate cannot be reached through words or mental activity, it is both expressible and inexpressible.

The principle does not differ in its fundamental aim. Generally speaking, although the four gates and four propositions may appear distinct when discussed according to the teachings, they are nonetheless interconnected.

Although there are various explanations regarding the shallow and the deep, or what is taught and what is not, when one reaches the ultimate, there is only the single, perfectly consummate, and ineffable state.

Nevertheless, for those at the initial stage of practice, there may be instances of gain or loss: if, like a swift horse seeing the shadow of a whip, one immediately enters the correct path, that is gain;
otherwise, one will become attached to words and grasp at them as mere frivolous discourse. If this is so, how can such things be valued as the primary meaning?
(50) The teaching arises from the wordless; yet without the wordless, there would be no way to manifest the subtlety of speech. Words explain the ultimate principle;
yet without speech, there would be no way to know the pinnacle of the wordless. This is why the Buddha constantly delights in silence, realizing that what is realized cannot be expressed.
Yet he could not help but speak, as he was constrained by the necessity of karmic conditions.

The reason Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth was that he had realized the principle of non-duality; it is something that can neither be reached through speech nor through the absence of speech, but is demonstrated solely through silence.
That this sutra cannot be proclaimed in words means that its principle is quiescent and transcends the reach of verbal distinctions.
As for the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* that "arising and so forth are ineffable," it refers to the same point.
This demonstrates that the teachings of the four *yānas* all originate in wordlessness;
therefore, by first employing words to dissolve them, all that is spoken becomes free from characteristics and utterly quiescent—how could it not then be dissolved?
Judging from this, although the wondrousness of non-speaking is one and the same, the underlying intent behind that non-speaking differs. This is what is meant by "having causes and conditions."
Therefore, it may also be said that according to our current interpretation, if sentient beings— who are constituted by the twelve links of dependent origination such as ignorance—
are approached by the Tathāgata and taught for the sake of the four kinds of aspiration, these also constitute the conditions for the four *siddhārtha* (purposes).

To explain the principle within phenomena for those of the sudden and perfect capacity can be called the ultimate. To speak of "all lands" refers to phenomena such as the environment and its inhabitants;
to speak of "Constant, Quiescent Light" refers to the principle. This is still an explanation based on differentiation;

if one does not grasp the essential intent, one merely knows that there are phenomena and a principle, yet remains unaware that phenomena are themselves the principle. Therefore, it is said: "Detached."

This "non-enlightenment" refers to the fact that phenomena are themselves the principle, with no separate principle apart from them. Precisely because there is no separate principle, it is permissible not to speak of the principle;
one may simply speak of phenomena, and the principle is contained therein. When the discourse reaches this point, it can be said that the ultimate limit of the perfect principle has been attained.
(55) Regarding the two paths of teaching and realization (*śāstra* and *adhigama*), within the fundamental gate of teaching, there is one difficult point fully explained in various commentaries.

What is stated here refers directly to the provisional and real, the pervasive and the limited, of the path of the separate teaching (*prthag-deśanā*).
