However, although the path of teaching is one, it is either pervasive or limited depending on the stages; or, alternatively, it may be considered as one.

Regarding the statement that "the beginning and end of the teaching constitute the path of teaching" (*jiaodao*), or alternatively that "the stages prior to the [ten] grounds constitute the path of teaching," there are indeed various explanations for each.

As for the view that "the beginning and end of one teaching" refers to this: it is precisely as the Tathāgata, within the various sūtras, speaks of the distinct teaching (*biejiao*), wherein there is only the path of teaching.

This is as when he says that the ten grounds are sequential and distinct, serving to lead those of lower capacities and acting as a skillful means for entering the grounds; this is what is called [the path of teaching].

To speak briefly, this refers to the Path of Teaching (*śāsana-mārga*). If one speaks from the perspective of the stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*), then because practice follows the position, the Path of Teaching is limited to the first thirty minds.
However, regarding the Path of Realization (*adhigama-mārga*) through practice, ascending the grounds is identical to the Perfect [Teaching].

Thus, there is a difference in their progression and regression. If one speaks from the perspective of the Path of Realization through practice, then pointing to the First Ground is precisely the phrase "the initial stage. This is it.
The meaning of these [teachings] is not different; if one can understand this discourse on teaching and realization (*śāsana-adhigama*), one has already grasped more than half of it.

This is detailed as in the *Lun* (Treatise). (Xuan Yi 56) The discourse on "opening up the provisional to reveal the real" is treated extensively in the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning); although the reasons for its exposition differ in each case, they are not... [incomplete].
To summarize the essential meaning of the principle that the substance is subtle while the phenomena are coarse, one finds that the majority of its significance is captured here.

As the current text states, "All dharmas are without exception subtle," this is spoken from the perspective of the fundamental source. Since the source itself is subtle, the provisional and the real among all dharmas are one and the same.
If they are not even to be considered identical, how could there be any difference? If they are not even to be considered distinct, what need is there for any further application [of teachings]?
There is indeed such a principle: those who establish provisional teachings as a practical expedient do so because the karmic conditions were not yet suitable for hearing this [ultimate truth].
Thus, for a period, they provide differentiated explanations; when sentient beings fail to understand these intentions, they cling to them as being real.

Now that the capacity for the Perfect [teaching] has matured, and one meets with the opening of the fundamental treatise, one realizes that the original wondrousness is not obtained from another. Therefore it is said: "The Dharma is fundamentally wondrous; coarseness arises only from the dispositions of sentient beings."
As for what this means: is "opening" the same as "opening," or is it different? One should investigate this deeply and will surely understand it for oneself.
Those who discuss the paths of the schools must not fail to distinguish between them; yet they must not exaggerate their distinctions. As for that which must be distinguished:

there may be errors in what has been transmitted or flaws in how things have been judged, and I fear these might mislead future students; therefore, one ought to distinguish them. However, even if one distinguishes them, one must not insist on changing [the tradition].

Alternatively, if the essential tenets have already been established, even if those [opponents] are capable of utterly abandoning what they have studied to follow me, it may be unnecessary to debate them;

in such a case, one might as well say, "Speak whatever brings you peace. However, those who cannot refrain from excessive debate likely give rise to contention regarding the Buddha-dharma, which is not the way to demonstrate the path of non-self.
Every time I read texts such as the *Zhanji* (Notes on the Commentary), I am reminded of this because of them.
Differences in judgment must be examined in detail; this is indeed the way of the Buddhist teachings, for fear that errors might mislead future students.
Rather than debating what would be of no benefit, it is better to allow them to transform themselves naturally; if one insists on correcting them directly, how difficult that would be!
(Section 34 of Xuan Yi) The citation of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* to show that the four *udānāni* are translated as "seals of tenets" (*zhongyin*) is intended to prove the error of the ancient masters.
While that particular translation may still be acceptable, it is certainly not permissible to translate *siddhānta* as "seals of tenets.
This is done merely because the phonetic sounds are close and their number is the same; yet, this fails to investigate the meaning of that text in relation to the current sense of *siddhānta*.

Because their meanings are entirely distinct, one knows they are not [the same]. Although this is not the primary intent of the text, the so-called four *udānās* are likewise not easy to clarify in terms of both wording and meaning.
(1.37) The *Shiqian* commentary explains that although that sutra belongs to the Mahāyāna, it intends to clarify the inclusion of all dharmas and is intended for beginners;
thus it merely speaks of practicing these four. Therefore, one knows they belong only to the Three Seals of the Hīnayāna teachings. Nevertheless, because...
In this passage, the dual explanation of both teaching and practice regarding the "seal" (mudrā) constitutes a definitive and immutable treatise;

furthermore, when it states, "that which was transmitted by the Buddha," and so forth, a detailed examination of its purport reveals that it does not refer merely to the Dharma-seal of the Hīnayāna. This is why it is difficult to clarify [the meaning].

I, however, say that this is not so. Generally speaking, what is called "Hīnayāna" refers to the beginning of gradual transformation; although it has not yet exhausted the full scope of the teachings and principles, [it nonetheless serves as a foundation].
If it were not for the Hīnayāna, the Mahāyāna could not be established; and if there were no precepts, concentration, and wisdom, there would likewise be no foundation for entering the Way.
This is precisely why the Great Sūtras uphold the Vinaya while discussing the Eternal (the Dharma-nature), and why all scriptural teachings must revere and honor them—it is for this very reason.
Thus, one knows that [the Vinaya] is the starting point of the Great Teaching and the orthodox lineage of the Buddha-dharma; how could it be otherwise?
As for the Way, later students have failed to comprehend it and have produced arguments of superiority and inferiority; how could they recognize the fundamental source of the Buddha’s transformation?

That which is "appropriate to its own level" means that the partial and the perfect, the Great and the Small, each remains within its own proper sphere without ever overstepping its bounds. To "leap across stages" [is to transcend these distinctions].

This refers to transcending those [distinctions] so that when one opens [the teaching], even the small is immediately perfect, with nothing that is not true reality; this is precisely what is meant by the current text.

However, as for the discussion regarding how the phenomena (相) are distinct while the principle (理) is fused—leaving behind the discourse on "easy" and "difficult"—it is as explained in the *Shi* (Commentary) at length.

This [current text] merely applies two meanings to address the questions and difficulties raised, but it has not yet explicitly stated their underlying intent. That intent, however, lies in the two subtleties of "provisional application" (*shi*) and "opening" (*kai*), and "waiting" (*dai*) and "transcendence" (*jue*).
This is the essential purport [of the teaching]. Therefore, it is said that one must understand the "appropriate division" (*dang-fen*) within a single era;

because it is understood throughout a single era, there are temporal distinctions between the present and the past, and doctrinal distinctions between the partial and the perfect—all of which pertain to their respective appropriate divisions.

Only the *Jinjing* (the Lotus Sūtra) transcends these stages; it reveals the coarseness of the Deer Park [teachings] as nothing other than the wondrousness of the *Jinjing*. It surpasses those two flavors and the two vehicles, for they do not exist within this [sūtra].
It is because they manifest entry [into the ultimate] that they receive their names; as for the Buddha’s intention, it fundamentally resides in the Great Pervasive [Teaching].

The three teachings of the preceding four periods all embody the meaning of "transcending the stages" (*kua jie*), not merely applying to the present alone. Speaking from this perspective, while each period was established according to its own respective stage in the past, the principle of "mutual dependence" applies to the present.

Thus, "transcending the stages" pertains only to the present when viewed in contrast to the past; yet when the present is made to pervade the past, this is what is called the Buddha’s intended teaching of "transcending the stages."
This is simply the purport of the present Sautrāntika school; there is no other doctrine.

Although [the terms] do not arise simultaneously and their expressions do not coincide—even if they occur in a sequence of before and after—they still cannot avoid being divergent. To speak of them in terms of actual reality, one cannot establish a priority or posteriority;
what this dharma is, that is the wondrous, and what this wondrous is, that is the dharma. They are non-dual and without distinction.

It may be so. Now, because we are speaking in terms of names and meanings, there is a mutual variation in their sequence. Thus, when the title designates "Sublime Dharma" (*Miaofa*), it follows the name;
when providing the explanation, it follows the meaning, and therefore places "Dharma" first and "Sublime" (*Miao*) last. Hence it is said:
"Although there is a variation in the sequence, they do not contradict one another. This is correct.
(Section 24 of Xuan) Whenever one critiques the ancients, if their arguments are not worth adopting, it is better to set them aside rather than discuss them;
if there are points within their doctrines that may be accepted, it is better to retain those acceptable elements while rejecting the unacceptable ones.
This is sufficient to demonstrate the fairness of one's own public judgment and to cause the opponent's shortcomings to be laid bare—this is something that must be understood.

(Section 24 of Xuán) Regarding the single character "mysterious" (*miào*) in the *Xuánwén*, the former commentary cites the explanations of several masters, stating: "It merely refutes [the views of] Guǎngzhái;

as for the others, they have followed suit based on the established doctrines concerning the causes and effects of the present and the past, which involve arguments of breadth and height, length and narrowness, and long and short.

It further states that twenty-four difficulties were raised against these, and so forth. Furthermore, Master Guān [Zhìyǐ] [analyzed them] by means of the three "non-[this]" and three "equal" categories.
To explain this for you now: it may be acceptable to say that on the first occasion, each was granted a partial understanding;
however, on the second occasion, when [the teaching] was taken away, although one might know the former through comparison and debate, one never spoke of how its wondrousness truly is.
As for the principle of "opening and revealing" (kaixian), it does not touch upon words at all; thus, there is nothing therein worth taking up, even when compared with Guangzhai. Its...
Although the meanings of "broad," "high," and "long" may seem applicable, there are many internal contradictions. For instance, it is said that the *Lotus Sūtra* does not clarify Buddha-nature;
yet when it speaks of the long duration of the Buddha's lifespan, it claims this is merely "unconditioned through the extension of life via supernatural powers.

This is a failure to understand the essential distinction between the provisional and the ultimate (the trace and the source). Such views effectively demote the *Lotus Sūtra* to the level of other scriptures—how can it then be said to be uniquely manifest?

How much more so, since they have not fully understood the teachings of the *Bhūmi* (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*) nor grasped the intent of the exclusive opening of the distinction [between the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles].

Therefore, it is appropriate that our school—by taking the past as the form and the present as the manifestation, and by asserting that the present is not the wondrous while the past is not coarse—should extensively demonstrate how their positions are entirely inverted;
and it is likewise fitting to refute them by examining the presence or absence of the "Fourfold One" (*shii*).
The *Giryaku* (Explanatory Examples) states: "Now, as for the contemplation of the mind (*kanjin*), there are three meanings; this is the first of them. (etc.

Furthermore, because the faculties and natures of those who practice the Dharma are rooted in the contemplation of the mind, and because there is no need to wait for specific practices, one may take whatever is seen or heard among phenomenal phenomena (*shihō*) and, by contemplating the object, bring it back to the mind.
Thus, one performs contemplation according to the text. Therefore, it is said: 'Following each phrase as it is heard,' and so forth."
If one phrase is thus, then every phrase is likewise; since it is said that "phenomena are subsumed," then every phenomenon is wondrous.
This means that in every word one perceives the Truth, and in every phrase one reaches the source; there is not a single dharma that does not accord with mind and object.

If one truly accords with all mind and objects, then object and contemplation will surely merge, and the Way will be attained. How profound! To subsume phenomena into principle is the true path of study and practice.

"This is the essential gateway for entering the Way"—these words originally originated from our own school; why then do you fail to reflect upon them and instead appropriate them for other uses? What a pity!
(From the *Xuanyi*, Fascicle 2)
(Section 20, Xuán) Where a doctrine is appropriate, it cannot fail to be adopted; where there is a deficiency in principle, it must be reformed.

As previously evaluated, the Guangzhai [Temple] represents a deficiency in principle and may thus be rejected; yet that which possesses a vast essence, a high status, and extensive utility represents what is appropriate in principle and may thus be employed.
Why is this? It is because the wondrous essence of the present sutra does not transcend these.
How could the ten realms and the three truths not be vast, lofty, and long? It is simply that others grasp their terminology but do not understand the reason for those words;
they possess the names but do not attain the reality behind them, and thus they are held in contempt by us today. Now that we have attained the reality, there is no fault in using their terminology.
Since the ten realms mutually embody the three truths in a state of fusion and identity, they do not transcend the single mind.

When there is no longer any distinction of before or after, nor of identity or difference, nor of unity or separation, then the wondrous purport is revealed; moreover, how could this concern merely names and realities?
Indeed, it is the nature of the Dharma that its essence is vast and its function is long-lasting, and it is the nature of the person that their station is high.

The person must be identical with the Dharma, and the Dharma must manifest the person; yet, that which mediates between them is the intent of "pervasive inclusion. It is precisely because one attains this [principle]...
Because it embodies both essence and function, its status is high; were its status not high, it would be insufficient to attain such essence and function.
Inferring from this, its significance is inexhaustible—this is why Tiantai excels in practical application and stands uniquely preeminent throughout antiquity and the present.

(Section 21: Profound) Now, the mind is but one; yet there are those that possess [the three thousand] and those that do not, those that are identical and those that are not, and those that are equal and those that are not.

This means that if it were not the Perfect Mind, the three thousand would not be subsumed; since the Perfect Mind is necessarily all-encompassing, how could the minds of the ten realms fail to possess them?
How could there be distinctions such as identity and non-identity, or equality and inequality? Therefore, its essence is vast and its function is long-reaching.
This wondrousness is also precisely the mind; there is no other dharma apart from it. If one discusses this mind, who among people does not possess it? What dharma is not so?

How could it wait for knowledge before becoming perfect, or for contemplation before becoming wondrous? Yet, as soon as a single thought of emotion arises, discrimination is triggered, and thus one cannot possess it—let alone be equal to it through such realization.
Nevertheless, if one realizes it directly right now, where would one go that is not [liberated]?

If one were to compare the present text with *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) to distinguish their similarities and differences, then the former is exhaustive in its detail while the latter is clear in its essential points;

yet, as for their sublime purport, they are no different. Furthermore, *Zhi guan* demonstrates [the nature] by way of the fundamental, making it easy to understand how the fundamental reveals the inherent presence (*ju*).
Here, however, we discuss by way of the derivative, taking it as essential to realize the substance through the derivative; therefore, we take the mind as the focus.
To thoroughly investigate all minds is to be equal to the Buddha-mind; by investigating with a mind equal to the Buddha-mind to its ultimate limit, one reaches the final fruition.

Although the functions appear to proceed sequentially, in principle they do not occur at different times; in a single thought-moment, perfect clarity manifests such that no phenomenon is not revealed.
The intent behind the instruction to "contemplate this" is indeed profound.

(Xuan 22) Previously, the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) and the three truths (*tisro satyāḥ*) were cited to demonstrate the wondrous; furthermore, the presence [of these] within one's own mind was observed to demonstrate contemplation.
This follows the method of Nanyue, who used these three dharmas to explain the Dharma, such that the upper and lower [levels] manifest one another.

Now, speaking in terms of the ten realms, although the mental dharmas (*dharmadhātu*) and the objective environment (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) are not explicitly opened up, they are indeed opened up within the dharma of sentient beings—this is what is meant by "causes."

Since the fruit and all dharmas are this [very same thing], one knows that the mutual opening and closing of the characteristics of dharmas constitute a single, wondrous essence that encompasses them all.
These three dharmas originally derive from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; they are now cited here to explain "wondrous" (*miao*).

Although the specific intent of those sections differs—distinguishing between what is opened and what is not—if one discusses them in general terms, they speak of "non-differentiation," whereas here the meaning is taken as the "wondrous Dharma. Therefore, [the two are consistent].

The wondrous is precisely the non-differentiated, and the non-differentiated is precisely the wondrous; yet, while speaking of non-differentiation does not necessarily manifest the wondrous, when we speak of the wondrous, its principle is necessarily non-differentiated.

Thus, one knows that "function" and "expediency" need not be treated as a single uniform category. Since this text clarifies the wondrous nature of the dharmas of sentient beings, it speaks in terms of the six sense faculties;
essentially, these do not transcend the principle of the Three Truths. In the present passage, it says: "The Buddha’s..."
In the *Zhijian*, the fleshly eye is identified with the five eyes; in the *Aṅgulimālīya*, it is said that they are fully possessed without deficiency;

in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that all dharmas tend toward equality. To clarify the subtlety of the Buddha-dharma, this is explained through the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real;

to clarify the subtlety of the mind-dharma, this is explained through the contemplation of the true mark of the mind. The principle is one and the same; one need only apply this intent to extend its application to other categories.

There is nothing that is not permissible. The names of the three dharmas were originally brief; now they are expanded by means of the causes and effects of the ten realms, giving rise to discussions regarding their universal application (*sāmānya*) or limited scope (*viśeṣa*).
Thus it is said, "and so forth": first, the name "sentient beings" (*sattva*) universally encompasses both the ordinary and the holy;

second, it is restricted solely to the nine realms and thus does not extend to the Buddha, nor does it apply to those who exist only in the causal stage—this serves to exclude non-mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).

Regarding the cause, this explanation is most direct; even other doctrines are but remote by comparison. Since it is said to "pervade all dharmas," these three present dharmas not only encompass the primary retribution but also extend to the supporting environment, thereby manifesting the subtle and comprehensive nature of this sutra regarding both the environment and the primary retribution.

Otherwise, how could it be said that the three thousand worlds are not spoken of, or that the provisional is not fully opened? If one discusses the fundamental nature of the mind-dharma, it likewise encompasses all.
To say generally that [the nature of] being determined resides in the cause is based on the fact that mental phenomena belong to oneself;

speaking in terms of the mind creating phenomena through its own conditions, one may thus use the mind as an analogy for the Buddha and others. Yet, how could those who claim that mental phenomena are not subject to cause and effect know this?

Furthermore, if we discuss each of the three dharmas—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—individually, then all three equally encompass both cause and effect, and may be used as analogies for one another.

Delusion and awakening should likewise be understood as mutually interpenetrating; yet, when considered from a restricted perspective, they ultimately return to the aforementioned principle (as stated at length).
The "interpenetration and restriction" of cause and effect refers to phenomenal function (*śakti*), while the "non-differentiation of the three" refers to the ontological essence (*svabhāva*).

Thus, the *Shu-chieh* (Sub-commentary) provides an explanation in terms of both ontological essence and phenomenal function, each corresponding precisely to its respective meaning. To speak of the non-differentiation of the ontological essence means that the three [bodies]—[the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya]—are without distinction.

Although phenomena differ, their single nature is equal; though there are distinctions between cause and effect, self and other, delusion and awakening, their fundamental rational nature (*li-xing*) is one.
Furthermore, it is said that "the mind creates" has two aspects; thus, each of the three dharmas possesses the three thousand [realms] in both fact (*shi*) and principle (*li*).

Therefore, while cause and effect are one in principle, how can self and other be different? Through the *Zhiguan*, these are unified to form the wondrous realm: the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment.

Therefore, it is said that [the meaning] is not yet understood; how can the present text be reconciled with these verses? For if one does not comprehend the marvel of the single mind’s possession of all phenomena (*dharmas*), how can one explain the principle of the non-differentiation of the three?
Although the underlying principle is consistent, the textual intent must be distinguished according to its sections.
First, in the general exposition of phenomena and principle, the three phenomena are treated as differentiated while their single nature is taken as non-differentiated; next, it concerns the creator.
When the mind is directed toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, three dharmas are established; each possesses two modes of "creation" (zào), which constitutes their distinction.

Since both modes of creation are encompassed, one must further distinguish them by taking "phenomenal creation" (shì-zào) as the point of differentiation and "principle creation" (lǐ-zào) as the point of non-differentiation.

If one follows the *Huìqǐ* commentary, then both principle and phenomenon include both principle and phenomenon, and both phenomenon and principle include both phenomenon and principle. Although these are mutually pervasive, each possesses two meanings that can both serve as points of differentiation.
There is no difference; that there is no difference means that the general purport is not distinct.

This is just as what the Four Ming masters call the "two levels of the general and the particular," both of which ultimately point back to the single thought-moment within phenomena. This perfectly accords with the intention of [Zhiyi’s] *Fuxing*.

If one says that the Buddha-dharma realm is already clarified as the three thousand [dharmas], it encompasses both the cause and the fruit, rather than being restricted solely to the fruit; it is nothing other than the Perfect [Teaching].
This is because of the nature of reality (dharmatā).

(Xuan 25) The three turnings of the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) and the merging and separation of the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*)—whether applied universally or specifically—are none other than the three truths (*tri-satya*).

This is because the essence of phenomena (*dharma-bhāva*) is perfectly wondrous; thus, when applied to words and meanings, they correspond to names and phrases, turning and transforming in every way without exception.
What can be done? Within this, one must give rise to definitive insight. If one attains this meaning, the three truths are inseparable.

To speak of "attaining the meaning" means that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is itself the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the middle (*madhyama*). When speaking of emptiness, it is the provisional that is identified as emptiness; when speaking of the provisional, it is by pointing to emptiness that the provisional is established;
when speaking of the middle, it is the extremes themselves that are called the middle. Therefore, all three are identical with the middle; thus, within the one, there is the middle.
Within all things, there is no emptiness that is not provisional, and no provisionality that is not empty; this principle applies universally.
From the perspective of self-negation, they are not one, two, or three; yet from the perspective of illumination, one, two, and three may also be called "overlapping and pervasive.

Although these expressions appear sequentially, they do not depart from a single thought-moment. It is for this reason that these Three Truths are neither vertical nor horizontal, and are thus termed the "True Aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Only the Buddha has exhausted [this truth] to its ultimate limit; how could it be reached by words or thought?
(Xuanzang 25) If one discusses the wondrous essence of the provisional and the real, it is simply that which the Buddha has realized—the three thousand worlds of Vairocana’s body and land.

How could there be any objective realm, intellect, or subject-object duality? Yet, to say that this is the object of the two wisdoms of all Buddhas is merely a provisional designation based on the cultivation of causes.

If one shows the fruit to those who are deluded and speaks from the perspective of the Buddha himself, the statement that "only the single true suchness-intelligence (tathatā-jñāna) remains" is indeed correct.
Furthermore, when the two wisdoms (prajñās) are applied throughout the three cycles [of the Lotus Sutra], it is said:

"All these are none other than the dharma of the provisional and the real regarding these ten 'thus-nesses' (yathābhūta). Thus, one should know that what is taught in both the "Original" and "Trace" gates throughout this entire scripture is likewise [this same principle].

How could it be that this [principle] transcends these? Since its principle has no fixed location and is omnipresent within all phenomena, the three thousand dharmas are none other than the true aspect (dharmatā).
Thus, the Buddhas have used it to reach ultimate manifestation; sentient beings rely upon it as their foundation; the mind-dharma takes it as its original wondrousness;
and this sutra uses it to reveal and clarify—these are all its essential purports. Students should especially apply their whole hearts to this.

(Section 29: The Pointing Finger) The wondrous realm indicated by the *Zhiguan* originates from the *Lotus Sūtra*; specifically, the "inconceivable realm" of *zhiguan*—the "three thousand worlds in a single thought-moment"—is fundamentally based on the passage concerning the "ten suchnesses" in this sūtra.
The text states: "If one does not speak of the ten suchnesses, cause and effect are incomplete.
Thus, the ten suchnesses are the phenomena of cause and effect; how could they alone suffice to serve as the "pointing finger"? Now, if we consider the first nine suchnesses...
The meaning of this remains general; one must point specifically to the single phrase "the ultimate equality of the beginning and the end" to perceive its true intent.
Why is this so? It means that regarding the beginning and the end, the reason why the nine suchnesses are all ultimately equal is precisely what the current text states:

"the place to which they return. Since it is called "the place to which they return," there is both the phenomenal (shi) and the principle (li). As for principle, the three thousand dharmas are all ultimately equal.

That which is called "equality" refers to the equality between the Buddha and sentient beings, the environment and its inhabitants, the provisional and the real, and from the initial marks to the final retribution—down to the very beginning and end.
There is not a single dharma that is not equal. The reason they are equal is simply because of the Three Truths. Therefore, one may designate this as the "wondrous object" (*miao-jing*);
the details are as shown elsewhere (etc.). If explained according to phenomena, it is what is referred to in the *Zhiguan* as the "ground."
The realm of hells takes the dharma of delusion as its ultimate; thus, by sequentially examining the ten realms, each is shown to have a specific dharma as its point of convergence (and so forth).

It is only through this that one first attains certainty regarding the respective points of convergence for the preceding nine realms, which are none other than the particular manifestations of this single "Suchness" (yiruo).
By clarifying this, one sees that there is nothing more essential than this investigation for pointing toward the ultimate of both phenomena and principle.
In the end, what else could the phrase "equal to the ultimate" (*jiǎngděng*) refer to if it were not based on this?
Furthermore, the text says: "If one does not rely on these three dharmas as being complete and ultimate, etc. If we discuss the three truths (*sandi*), all are inconceivable (*bùsīyì*);
how could it be that one is so and two are not? This is merely a provisional way of using the term "ultimate" in contrast to the two truths; in reality, it refers to the three.
Only when all are ultimately perfected can they be called "equal"; how could there be any taking or rejecting among them? (Xuanzang, Vol. 2, p.

32) The subtlety of the three contemplations merges back into the one mind; it does not depart from a single thought-moment, yet the three phases appear. This principle is difficult to clarify and the human intellect is not easily enlightened;
I shall now illustrate it through the metaphor of a dream so that you may gain a rough approximation. The text says: "As in a dream..."

When one cultivates the cause and attains the fruit within the middle way, one knows that dream-events encompass both the fundamental and the derivative; since they all appear vividly, are they not provisional?
Since none of them can be apprehended, are they not empty? Since the nature of the mind in a dream is neither existent nor empty, is it not the Middle Way?
Such distinctions occur in a single moment; therefore, there is no sequence of before or after, nor is there identity or difference, and thus they are not conjoined.
If one scatters [the seeds], how could such a nature not be considered non-sublime?
(Xuan 2.20) Regarding the cultivation of good and evil natures, this is also a point of significance within the teachings.

According to the *Xuánshì* (Explanations of the Profound), it is said that among these natures, the "nature of the four miserable destinies" refers to the meaning of a black, self-contained nature (*kṛṣṇa-svabhāva*) because they purely habituate themselves to evil karma; thus, they are difficult to transform.

"Wood has the nature of fire," etc.—this statement regarding "nature" refers to the nature of one's allotted lot (*xing-fen*), which is what is meant by the phrase "long-term habituation forms a nature. (Section 2, 37) The commentary on the fascicle explains that because of the statement "it cannot be changed," it says: "In terms of principle, the nature that is originally present (*ben-you*) cannot be changed; in terms of cultivation, the nature of one's allotted lot cannot be changed. Thus, this further includes the nature that is originally present. As for "nature": 1. It is the nature of the Dharma-realm, which is the true suchness of all phenomena. 2. It is the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha, which is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings. 3. It is the nature of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which is the Buddha-nature of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. 4. It is the nature of the five aggregates, which is the Buddha-nature of ordinary beings. 5. It is the nature of the mind, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have not yet awakened. 6. It is the nature of the six consciousnesses, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have already awakened. 7. It is the nature of the six sense objects, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have attained the fruit. 8. It is the nature of the six sense organs, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have entered the path. 9. It is the nature of the six sense fields, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have realized the truth. 10. It is the nature of the six sense faculties, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have completed their practice. 11. It is the nature of the six sense powers, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have reached the ultimate. 12. It is the nature of the six sense functions, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have perfected their realization. 13. It is the nature of the six sense activities, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have attained mastery. 14. It is the nature of the six sense transformations, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have attained liberation. 15. It is the nature of the six sense manifestations, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have attained the fruit of Buddhahood. 16. It is the nature of the six sense harmonies, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have attained the harmony of the three bodies. 17. It is the nature of the six sense integrations, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have attained the integration of the ten directions. 18. It is the nature of the six sense pervasions, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have attained the pervasion of the Dharma-realm. 19. It is the nature of the six sense fulfillments, which is the Buddha-nature of those who have fulfilled all vows. 20. Within the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), there is the "contracted observation" (*saṃkṣipta-vipaśyanā*). "Contraction" means reduction; starting from the first object of the two upper realms, one reduces it by one.
In this manner, proceeding from the end toward the beginning, one gradually reduces them in successive stages. Thus, after seven cycles of reducing the objects, twenty [aspects] remain.
When the reductions in all four aspects have been completed, they are no longer employed; until only one aspect and one object remain, this is called the stage of medium patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*).

When the remainder reaches the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), proceeding from this single aspect and single object toward the true insight of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), this is called the stage of supreme patience.
Thereafter, beneath each of the four truths, one generates one patience and one knowledge; when these sixteen moments of mind are fulfilled, one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The general characteristics of the contemplative practice at this stage are roughly as described above;

regarding other textual passages that may expand or contract, advance or retreat, or increase or decrease, they should be understood according to their respective meanings, and thus I shall omit them here for brevity. To use an analogy:
suppose a person has accumulated vast wealth and wishes to travel to another country but cannot carry it all with them; they therefore exchange their goods for gold, and then for gold [coins].

The principle of the gradual depletion of the treasures of the *Yi* is likewise in its manifestation. Now, if the Great Teaching directly penetrates to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally empty, how could there be any迂闊 (redundancy or circuitousness)?
Why then is it that one cannot accept and take responsibility for this? Someone asked: "What is the characteristic of the true illumination of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*)?
This is like a worldly person extinguishing fire to produce charcoal, leaving behind only a single bean-sized spark of the fire-seed. And...

When blown away and extinguished by the wind, it blazes out and leaves nothing remaining; even this seed comes to no longer exist. By means of this metaphor, the application to the Dharma can be understood.

(Section 51 of Volume 3 of the Xuánzàng Translation) The text cites two sutras to demonstrate the profundity of the merits of the five stages (*pañca-varga*).

As for how one can remain uninterrupted yet be pure and complete, and how one can harbor delusions yet possess knowledge—it is because the afflictions of the five desires are the obstacles, whereas the purification of the sense faculties is the means.
To be able to know the treasury of principle is virtue; the obstacle to the perfect expression of this principle is but one.

When a person of perfect capacity embodies it, the very obstacle manifests as virtue; thus, they are able to remain uninterrupted while being detached, and in that state of detachment, they purify the sense faculties.
Realizing that afflictions are nothing other than the inherent nature, this state of inherent nature is the secret treasury, wherein there is no other dharma to be apprehended.
This refers to what is manifested. If there were truly a severance [of delusion], then conceptual discrimination would still persist and emotional perceptions would not have perished;
how could this be considered the practice of the perfect and subtle contemplation? If the stages of practice are such as these, it is fitting that he be the master and patriarch of this school.
Based on what was previously clarified, wisdom illuminates the object, and wisdom is generated because of the object; this is indeed the general principle regarding object and wisdom. Furthermore—
The nature of dharmas is such that it cannot be altered; yet, once these four propositions fall into the grasping of a fixed nature, they become nothing more than false conceptualizations.

This is erroneous and mistaken; how can one hope to enter into the principle? What is meant is that while one’s own practice is already free from the four attachments, there is no hindrance to teaching others through the four modes of exposition.
Within that objective realm and wisdom, there is from the outset no real dharma. Since there is no real dharma, there is no fixed attachment;

thus, there is no impediment to that which illuminates, which is wisdom, nor to that which is illuminated, which is the objective realm. This may also be understood according to the analogy of "burning and illuminating."
When the inconceivable realm that is elucidated illuminates the four phrases beginning with "wisdom," the mind and object are both revealed;

All are but empty-fisted deceptions used to entice the small-minded; at the time of wondrous realization, not a single dharma can be obtained, and it may simply be said that this is neither provisional nor real.

(Numinous Verse 3716, Divination Slip 311) Generally, when a school establishes itself, it relies upon the teachings as its basis; whether in affirming, negating, refuting, or reconciling, none is more detailed than this [text].

As for why the ancient masters erred, they erred due to partiality.

Zan’s propagation merely asserted a single gate while losing the grand principle; he intermingled secular texts with ornate embellishments, thereby causing the pure and ultimate flavor to become disordered.

This was not as good as my ancestor Daoyue, who, within a single generation of the teaching gate, expounded the purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* by universally refuting and establishing, refuting the provisional to establish the definitive, and establishing the provisional through refutation. Regarding the claim that the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* represents the ultimate by transcending words, and the assertion that the present section cannot be considered "sublime," how should scholars resolve these points?

(Xuanzang’s Commentary, Vol. 4, Part 1) The tenfold "Sublimity" (*daśa-prakāra-miṣṭha*) arises from the principles of the Dharma; its application is both universal and specific. One must not generalize the distinctions between the coarse and the sublime. Herein, we clarify the arising of the Dharma.

Regarding the third set of dharmas, their characteristics must accord with both principle and phenomena; yet, when the text dismisses them as not being "sublime," it is merely setting aside their fixed formulation in order to contrast it with the perfect fusion of the three and the one. It does not mean that they are ultimately not sublime.

Since it is said that one should understand according to the characteristics of the dharmas and practice according to what has been taught, one knows that the three objects (*viṣaya*) are identical to the three wisdoms (*jñāna*), and the three wisdoms are identical to the three practices (*caryā*).
Each of the three [principles] possesses its own three dharmas, like the letter *i* or the third eye of Śiva; how could anything fail to be the wondrous essence?

As for the discussion of the characteristics and penetration of these dharmas, it is said: "Now we clarify that practitioners mostly abide in the stage prior to the [ten] abodes," and "The object is itself the nature of the object, the three virtues, etc.

In the end, how could one possibly occupy a fixed position? This is like the case of Siming’s *Explanation of the Gate of Non-duality*, which discusses the union and separation of cultivation and nature (*xiuxing*) while prioritizing the clarification of the ten kinds of threefold dharmas (*shizhong sanfa*) that encompass both the beginning and the end. this can be understood from the introductory remarks and the appended annotations.

(Xuan 45) It is explained that all dharmas have a single characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless. Furthermore, the use of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as a metaphor is profound indeed;

Moreover, by using the single characteristic to refute diverse characteristics, [the truth is revealed] hereafter.

By using the signless (*animitta*) to shatter the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), such that the single characteristic becomes unattainable, one can then universally penetrate the characteristics of all phenomena.
Thus, the so-called "gate of contemplation on non-arising" (*anutpāda-vipaśyanā-mukha*) is attained.

Furthermore, by taking the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as proposed in the *Avalokiteśvara-paripṛcchā* and explaining them together, one reveals the meaning of shattering both afflictive emotions (*kleśa*) and dharmas; when this finally returns to the signless, one enters [the ultimate truth].
What method could there be for the essentials of the Way other than this? Therefore, those who study and practice should especially strive to realize it through personal experience.

(Xuan 4.6) Now, taking the entry of Sudhana into the Dharma-realm as distinct, incremental practices—taking what the scripture calls "I only know this dharma-gate" as these successive acts—is because the ignorance that is thereby destroyed is the ignorance of non-knowing.

*The Profound Meaning*, Fascicle 4 (Xuan 4.23):

Regarding the statement that "the samādhi of universal illumination (*sāmānyāloka*) is one of the three grades of the fundamental pure dhyāna, and its nature is that of concentration and wisdom," this refers to the method of the Universal Illumination Contemplation (*sāmānyāloka-vipaśyanā*).
Because it is profound and subtle, it is capable of giving rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state; thus, the passage on "maintaining joy" says: "discerning the truths."

To contemplate the inhalation and exhalation of the breath is the contemplation of the breath (*ānāpāna*). To observe that the body fundamentally does not exist, down to its four subtle elements (*paramāṇu*), each of which is not the body, is the contemplation of the body (*kāya*).
To contemplate that the body arises from the mind, and the mind arises from conditions (*pratyaya*), and so forth, is the contemplation of the mind (*citta*).

When such contemplations are perfected, their characteristics are neither three distinct natures nor different; yet they cannot be said to have a single characteristic either. Since they are neither one nor different, they cannot be apprehended.
Are not all phenomena empty? Therefore, by internally realizing true emptiness, one knows that the celestial bodies, the patterns of heaven, and the geography of the earth correspond to the body.
This is precisely the principle referred to by those of antiquity who said: "To turn back upon oneself and find sincerity—there is no joy greater than this.
How much more so when, by means of this, one can destroy delusions, realize the truth, and attain the *nirvāṇa* of the Three Vehicles! Thus, one should know that this Dharma is supreme.

It is concise and essential; if one can cultivate this accord, what could be more wondrous? Yet it cannot be called easy, nor can it be called difficult—it depends entirely on how one applies oneself to practice.

Generally, whenever a great sutra speaks of dharmas in terms of the ultimate, it invariably says so.
(Section 4, Item 31) The terms "mind" (*citta*) and "nature" (*prakṛti*) are not easily distinguished; now, taking the mind as its own nature—this is what is meant by "the nature of all minds.

From the mind and its mental factors, this mind encompasses all phenomena, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel does; for their essence is fundamentally one.
Because their essence is fundamentally one, there are no phenomena that are not the Dharma-realm. All phenomena tend toward dhyāna, and outside of dhyāna there is nothing else.
To encounter an object is immediately the truth; a single form and a single mind are none other than the Middle Way—all of this is this principle. As it is said:

32) Furthermore, while the five practices (*pañca-caryā*) originate from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the four truths (*catvāri satyāni*) are all situated within the Separate Teaching (*prthag-deśanā*). This horizontally encompasses the four teachings and vertically distinguishes the various stages.

Therefore, I now cite from the *Prajñāpāramitā* up to the ultimate of *Nirvāṇa*, for all Buddhas...
Nothing emerges from illusion and transformation that has ever possessed reality, because both of these dharmas arise from false dharmas;

Regarding its meaning (as elaborated above):

[Quotation from Fascicle 4, Section 48] "The provisional nature of the teaching and the reality of the principle—this meaning is somewhat difficult to comprehend; this is precisely why it differs from other teachings.

Now, in clarifying the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), there are statements regarding the mutual identity of affliction and awakening. Now, regarding the provisional nature of the teaching from the perspective of the cause: from the standpoint of the initial mind, there is only the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*).

Therefore, there are statements such as "extensively gathering the Buddha-dharma," whose actual meaning derives from the fruit; according to the purport of the teaching, this results in non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).

Thus, there is the explanation that this is solely the intended meaning of this teaching. In this way, while the provisional and the real aspects of the teaching may appear on the surface to be contradictory, their meanings do not exclude one another;

(Verse 448) It further states: "Thus we know that 'vertical progression,' 'staying in practice,' and 'stillness' likewise involve delusion regarding the equal and correct [enlightenment]. (Section 4, 36) Regarding the meaning of the essence and function of "obscuration" (*zhē*) and "illumination" (*zhào*), there is already a settled doctrine in various texts; yet, in this particular passage, it is stated that "there are four [aspects]," and so forth.

Taking the mark of quiescent extinction (*jìmíèxiàng*) as both obscuring and negating, and taking the marks of active functioning (*xínglèixiàngmào*) as both flowing and illuminating, the meaning is perfectly consistent.
(Section 4, 50) The *Shì* commentary states: "Obscuration and flowing pertain to the function of wisdom (*zhìyòng*); negation and illumination pertain to the essence of wisdom (*zhìtǐ*)."

Each [aspect] possesses both essence and function; it is not merely a matter of the meanings of "exclusion" (*zhē*) and "illumination" (*zhào*), but also involves the intermingling of essence and function.

What is the underlying principle here? Now, I maintain that there is a specific reason: it is simply because the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) discusses "exclusion as the cessation of flux" and "illumination as the layering of manifestations" in such a way that they seem redundant.
Therefore, the *Qiān* (Sub-commentary) specifically distinguishes their principles by stating "each has one essence" and "each has one function. As for what preceded this, its words were omitted.
It may be said that its function can be understood through its essence; why then is it considered strange that its obscuring and illuminating aspects are reversed?

We reply: this is not difficult at all, yet people remain stubbornly deluded. To call "obscuring" the act of veiling confusion—is this not its function? To take "illuminating" as the grasping of the nature of illumination—is this not its essence?

Thus, not only does the text avoid redundancy, but it also clearly demonstrates that essence and function each possess their own distinct character, such that the principle flows with ease. This is the interpretation of the text.
This is skillful; the remainder is excluded, as the chapter reveals this.

(Xuan 4.40) The text clarifies that in the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), one realizes the King Samādhi (*rāja-samādhi*), which can shatter all modes of existence (*bhava*) and attain the names of twenty-five samādhis.
Although the text is verbose, its essential purport can be summarized briefly into four points: namely, that within each mode of existence there are three afflictions (*kleśa*).

First, the faults of karmic characteristics are one [point]. Second, because Bodhisattvas resolve to cultivate Brahma-like and noble practices in order to destroy the faults of themselves and others, this constitutes the merit of the fundamental dharma.
Third, once the three delusions and karmic characteristics have been destroyed, they realize the Three Truths;
thus, the completion of their practice constitutes samādhi. Subsequently, they utilize the fundamental great vows to permeate and transform the Dharma through subtle influence.

If there are sentient beings with the karmic conditions to be related to through compassion, the Bodhisattva, by means of the power of the King Samādhi, responds to them without moving from the *dharmatā*, causing them to attain this realization;
thus, through the ultimate perfection of compassion, the four [marks] are destroyed. This is merely the general outline.

Regarding this, there are two difficult points for discussion: first, it is said that karma, as well as the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*), are what are destroyed within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The interpretation of this is found in the *Sijian daming da Riben wen zhang* (Chapter on the Response to Japanese Questions). It further clarifies that through the realization of the two emptinesses, one attains the wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional. Regarding the presence or absence of the "flame" (*jiaoyan*), there are other texts;
as for the differences in the meaning of the truths (*diyi*), they are as explained in the *Leilun* (Treatise on Categories), and so forth.
(Section 42 of Xuan) The teaching of the mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru is difficult to comprehend through emotional discrimination, yet easy to clarify through principle.
This is because the single nature is equal and fundamentally neither small nor large; thus, the mustard seed is not small and Mount Sumeru is not large.

Now, that which is "large" by virtue of being non-large enters into that which is "small" by virtue of being non-small, and that which is "small" by virtue of being non-small contains that which is "large" by virtue of being non-large.

Although they enter [the realm of phenomena] without obstruction, because each phenomenon does not lose its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), they do not harm grasses or trees, nor do they burn fish or turtles;
the two original natures remain exactly as they were. This is what is called the inconceivable true nature of liberation.
Because Bodhisattvas realize this nature within all phenomena, they attain this wondrous function of liberation; indeed, there is no room for doubt regarding this essential point.
One should believe and revere the teachings and rely upon the principle; one ought not to obscure oneself with emotional conceptions and thereby lose the path to the fundamental source.
Otherwise, you will deceive yourself.

(Xuanyuan 4.65) The Way has neither coarseness nor subtlety; it is through the teachings that coarseness and subtlety arise. The Dharma has neither loss nor gain; it is because of people that loss and gain occur.
Therefore, this dialogue states: "If one discusses the single path of purity, it has never from the beginning possessed any difference;

yet, when it was bestowed in the past, it was considered coarse, while when it is revealed now, it is considered subtle. Because it remains to accommodate future conditions, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* further speaks of partial and gradual [teachings].

This distinction between the coarseness and subtlety of the teaching is also the distinction between the provisional and the real of the Dharma. Nevertheless, the Dharma itself possesses no increase."
Because of this potential for harm, one need not necessarily lose the provisional (upāya) nor necessarily gain the ultimate (paramārtha); it is simply a matter of what is appropriate.

Thus, in the past, the *Lotus Sūtra* was used to manifest the ultimate while the provisional was deemed appropriate; once the ultimate was revealed, there was no longer anything crude about it, and the Buddha’s intention for teaching during his lifetime was thereby fulfilled.

However, those in the final age who do not grasp this intent may either cling to the ultimate and discard the provisional, or mistake the provisional for the ultimate—even if they consume the *amṛta* (clarified butter).
When poison is formed, it cannot immediately manifest the truth through the matter at hand; consequently, it causes injury to life and premature death.
To cause harm to people is not what is meant by the Dharma; this is precisely why the teaching of the *Nirvāṇa* was established.

As for those who speak of "supporting" (*fu*) precept, concentration, and wisdom, some say it means "supporting the rules (*lǜ*) while discussing the eternal (*cháng*)," which is merely a matter of detail or brevity. In reality, the merit of supporting and manifesting [the truth] cannot be achieved without these three.

(Emei 4.77) Regarding the statement that after the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) one "repeatedly contemplates the truth" (*punar-vicāraṇa-tattva-ālambana*): this means that one repeatedly takes as an object of contemplation the truth previously realized and subsequently abandons the afflictions of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

This so-called "further cultivation of the sixteen aspects of the truths" (*ṣoḍaśākāra-satyadarśana-bhāvanā*) is explained according to the previous [system], which refers merely to contemplating the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) underlying each of the truths.
(Emei 4.78) Furthermore, it says: "From abandoning one grade of desire-afflictions (*kāmāsrava-prakāra*) up to abandoning five grades," according to the school of this treatise (*śāstra*).

Regarding the "householder" (kulaṃkula), according to what is clarified in the treatises, it should be discussed in terms of severing three or four grades [of afflictions]. That it is now said to extend to five grades is a general statement based on this specific context;

it does not mean that [the householder] must sever all five grades. This is as explained in the *Zhiguan* regarding the meaning of the "householder" in terms of the two faculties—the transcendent and the gradual—wherein the commentary points out:
"This refers to those who sever [afflictions gradually]" (*cì duàn*). This likely captures the true intent of the present text. For further details, see [the relevant sections].
In another treatise (and so forth), it says:

"The term 'various ways' (*bān bān*) refers to those who attain *parinirvāṇa* after the third fruit; because their root-natures (*indriya-gotra*) follow many paths, the word is repeated to encompass them all.

Regarding the differences in the ancient commentaries, there are two points: first, the *Abhidharmakośa* does not establish the existence of one who attains *parinirvāṇa* in the present life; second, it clarifies that... [text fragment].
The details regarding the fixed nature of these [attainments] are as explained in the *Yìzhāng* (Chapter on Meaning);

there is no need for further elaboration here. (Xuanzang’s translation, Vol. 4, p. 79) The fetters pertaining to the upper and lower realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya* and *adharabhāgīya*) are fundamentally not very difficult to understand. However, since delusions are categorized according to their respective realms, they are divided into "upper" and "lower.

Specifically, the view-fetters (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) along with the desire-fetters (*kāma-rāga*) and the aversion-fetters (*pratigha*) belong to the lower realm; all others belong to the upper realm. Therefore, it is said that while three fetters are mentioned briefly, they are explained extensively [in the scriptures].

Regarding the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), three fetters (*saṃyojana*) belong to the category of views (*dṛṣṭi*), while the remaining seven belong to the category of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and so forth.

However, although it is said that the proclivities of view generally pervade all three realms, their classification as "lower-fettering" (*avarabhāgīya*) is merely in terms of their role in drawing one back into rebirth. As it is said: "By two [fetters], one does not transcend the desire realm;

by three, one returns to the lower [realms]. Furthermore, it is stated: "Even if one has severed greed and the other [defilements] up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one still returns due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the others."
That they return to the lower realms is precisely this point. Having already pervaded the three realms, why is it that rebirth is drawn only toward the lower?

It is said that the deviant and the correct are not the same. When views are deviant, the three poisons are heavy and one is drawn into the four destinies; when volitional thoughts are correct, the three poisons are light and one is bound to the human and celestial realms.

Knowing this, one understands the general path of the four abiding delusions (*catur-vāsa-kleśa*) and the essential points of the fivefold fetters (*pañca-bandhana*). Furthermore, as for the preceding text:
It is said: "The nineteen proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms, both sharp and dull, refer precisely to the proclivities that take cessation as their object;
this is stated by specifically focusing on the proclivities of the afflictions belonging to the Truth of Cessation. (And so forth.)

(Section 4813, Volume Xuan) As for why the Pratyekabuddha is called the Middle Vehicle, it is because they occupy a position between the Śrāvaka and the Bodhisattva. Because their faculties (*indriya*) are sharp, they rank above the Śrāvaka;

because they seek only their own liberation, they rank below the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, there is the distinction between encountering a Buddha in the world and not encountering one, which likewise arises from the nature of their faculties, their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Nevertheless, due to their sharp faculties and profound merit, they are certain to encounter a Buddha.
That he alone appeared in an age without a Buddha suggests that his innate nature was characterized by much arrogance;
thus, although he attained awakening to non-arising and entered the stream of the sages, he ultimately remained hindered by this innate pride.

Otherwise, how could it be that knowing a Buddha had appeared in the world, he first manifested himself as a transformed body or was moved elsewhere, being compared to a comet? Only then can one recognize the obstruction of his innate nature.

Since even the sages could not avoid being difficult to move from [their state], how much more so those of ordinary and inferior capacity? Therefore, this is discussed as a warning for those who are conceited regarding their superior status.

As for the realization of the fruit, it is no different from that of the pratyekabuddhas; however, since there are also those among the pratyekabuddhas who previously dwelt on the stages of training (śaikṣabhūmi) during the causal stage, they possess inherently sharp faculties and do not necessarily have to attain the fruit [only after completing the path]. Thus, this case is distinct from that.

As for the section on the Qilin (the auspicious beast), its metaphors regarding the categories of those capable or incapable of practicing supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and preaching the Dharma cannot be fully exhausted here (and so forth). (Xuanzang, Vol.

48, p. 14) The fundamental purpose of the Tripiṭaka Teaching is primarily for the Two Vehicles, while it incidentally accommodates Bodhisattvas; because it employs concealed characteristics (*saṃvṛti-lakṣaṇa*), it does not discuss the destruction of delusions.

To leave the realm of conditioned existence and, being urgent in benefiting others, to subdue afflictions, cultivate causal practices, and bring mundane virtues to rest—this is merely the preliminary stage.

As for the completion of practice and the perfection of the fruit, wherein one gives rise to wisdom, shatters delusions, and attains the Bodhi of Buddhahood—this constitutes the characteristics of the beginning and the end.

Discussed from this perspective, the three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and hundred kalpas, the four stages of attaining the Way, and the various Mahāyāna sūtras elucidating the bodhisattva stages [are all consistent].

It is certainly impossible to speak of these as being on the same level; yet, it is incorrect for the masters of antiquity to state in general that Bodhisattvas do not distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles.

Thus, from the initial generation of the mind through the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, if one compares this to the stages of the Śrāvakas, it corresponds to the seven levels of the *pṛthagjana* (the Seven Worthies).

Therefore, it is clear that at the causal stage, the discussion does not concern the severance of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*). There is no need for further convoluted analysis. As for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
The refutation of the intent of the *Quanbu* (Section on Authority) regarding the establishment and negation of existence and non-existence is detailed in a separate treatise (*yun yun*).

(Xuan 48.88) There are generally four points commonly discussed regarding the stages of penetration (*tongwei*): first, the separate establishment of the name "patience" (*ren*); second, the progression or non-progression in relation to the stages;
third, the wick-flame of the initial resolve; and fourth, the ten stages being like those of a Buddha. Regarding the so-called "separate establishment of the name 'patience'":
This refers to the fact that throughout the beginning and end of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of this teaching, these practices are common to all three vehicles;

yet, although Bodhisattvas likewise destroy delusions, realize the truth, give rise to no grasping or attachment, subdue their minds, sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and purify Buddha-lands, they excel in ways that the two vehicles cannot match.
Therefore, names such as "Subduing Patience" (*kṣānti*) are specifically bestowed upon them to praise them. Thus it is said: [The Great...]

A treatise states: "What is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavipaśyanā-bhūmi*) within the *Śrāvaka* Dharma is, for a Bodhisattva, precisely the Patience of Subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*)," and this is its meaning.

(Xuanzang, Vol. 49, p. 12). Second, regarding the advancement or non-advancement by borrowing stages: according to the current text and the *Mohe Zhiguan*, their characteristics are detailed [as follows]... and the text [continues].
There are three or four instances where the meanings of borrowed terms differ; previous scholars have all discussed these without reaching a definitive conclusion.

My current discussion offers nothing new, for it simply fails to distinguish between that which is borrowed and that which is designated by the name. However, if one follows the designation from what is borrowed, there are three cases:

first, borrowing the entirety [of a teaching] while sharing the names of its beginning and end across positions; second, borrowing a single [element] while designating it as distinct from the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); and third, borrowing a subsequent [element] while designating it as distinct.
Since those named as "Bodhisattvas who have attained the stage" constitute three types of borrowing, if one were to follow the names from the perspective of what is borrowed, there would be only two;

therefore, the texts on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* list only two types of borrowing. Although the text mentions that the distinct vision of the meaning is extensive and so forth, this merely follows the latter [classification], as the text states that these eight persons belong to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). Thus, it is unnecessary to establish them separately. However...

Having made this judgment, the number is fixed. Now, to further clarify its characteristics, I shall again illustrate it by borrowing the meaning of the "Perfect One" (Yuan-yi) from the list of names;

thus, its aspects will become clear. As the text says at length: in essence, although the stages are established according to the scriptures and treatises, because the textual characteristics themselves also present difficulties for a definitive judgment, I have merely clarified them by means of borrowed meanings. This is also the living method of textual interpretation employed within our own school.
The remaining three or four meanings are explained elsewhere (etc.).
End of Volume Lower of the *Miaoxuan* (Exquisite Profundity), a collection of aphorisms from the Great Treatise.
